game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is simple:
It's a game where you play a investigator who works for the government, sifting through data in all of its forms in order to fight for the safety of the public in the fictional world that it's set in.

There have been many 'hacking' games that have come out over the years, but Orwell takes the idea and puts you in the position of 'good' rather than 'bad', which creates the core ideology of the game -- If what you're doing is so good, then why do you feel so bad doing it?

The game proceeds along a UI of sorts, one that allows you to sift through websites, personal pages and even listen on some incredibly well-simulated 'real time chats', along with interruptions and intentional spelling errors that betray the typer's emotions and mental states. It's one of the best simulations of texting I've seen before in a game, and it DOES stand out. The articles and websites, while simple and clean, are detailed and packed full of worldbuilding -- the developers go out of their way to fill the world with detail that was never necessary to get from point A to B, but still fill everything with life and activity, and the world ends up feeling a little bit less compartmentalized than other games which force you into a limited POV.

However, this all leads back to the internal condundrum I have with this game:
You work with a handler who analyses the information you send him, and it's his job to make sense of it all. All you do is forward him the pertinent information, enough for him to make decisions and calls on how to handle situations. And you must choose what it is you want to send.

It's your choice to pick A over B. And it's not outright lies, because you're the good guy, remember? But whatever you send can tinge a thought, affect outcomes and colour perceptions in slight, yet pertinent, ways. Your own analysis plays a big part in how you want to portray someone else, and ultimately, the only one who has to live with the decisions you make is yourself.

Orwell is a great game about people, but more than that, it's a platform to help you examine yourself as a person. Since you're doing this for the percieved good, what decisions will you make and how far will you go to get what you want? And is there ever a time when personal freedom can be infringed upon for the greater result? Well... that might be another question for another time.

It's a good game tho, eh?

(( P.S.: Like any other 'visual novel' style game, and including the horrendous works of Mr. David Cage, I am fully aware that some of these 'choices' may be nothing more than illusionary. However, the game does it well enough in its context that reflecting upon the choices you make actually makes more than just a surface-level difference since you're playing not a character, but yourself. And considering the game's name and influences, I believe this to be the point. ))

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

11/10 would hack the local fishing society again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

review_text_raw:
The creation of the internet is the most technological advance tool mankind has ever made, right next to toilets. With the modern age of technology we have today, the effects on our lives stack up as the age-old question Security vs. Freedom comes into the debate again.  I am talking about a game where it tackles the subject on privacy issues which is Orwell. There will be a spoiler section on the comments to give my personal thoughts on some episodes. I will give an analytical review of this game and give in my two cents if this plays well as it was intended. 

[h1]CHECKING YOUR ID[/h1]

You play as Snowden-I MEAN the investigator, you work for the government and try a new technology called Orwell. You checked on people’s devices and try to add data chunks that matter on a case you are specifically working on. To be frank, in the first episode I was intrigued by the concept of the machine, it felt the game was really inspired by the true story of Edward Snowden about the CIA scandal. Now, the difference from the actual real event and the game is that the game focus on only the investigator and your co-worker trying to solve this case together. You the investigator only see the dirty secrets while your advisor Symes only advice you on your next tasks or comment on your search. I will explain a bit more detail but it will have to be in the spoiler section on why Orwell works like that.

[h1]BACKGROUND CHARACTERS AND STORY[/h1]

I have to cut a lot to avoid spoilers so I will give you a summary of the story but will give you how the characters and their world behave. The story is interesting for how it was trying to show the concept of privacy. I absolutely love how each character from the profiles you investigate shows a unique dialogue from each text you read from different characters. They feel almost exactly like how people should talk especially on the internet. When you read each email, phone calls etc. you can picture actual people having a real conversation which is great! It never made you feel like the dialogue felt artificial or fake, like adults “trying” to sound what people would say on the internet. I also love how they try to implement how people would sound like on the comment sections and insert memes along the way. 

The art style is another unique aspect of the game of how it shows a polygonal art style look. Most of the faces are fine though some were not as quite good in certain looks like some faces of the characters you profile are a bit strange with their beady eyes or mouth. The music is quite good giving you a sense of futuristic vibe to it while also gives you a dread feeling where certain events happen during your case. You even have one shot whatever you send data chunks to Symes and you can’t go back to it even exit the game won’t do. Whatever you send to Symes will affect the characters that you are working on the case. Which now I will talk about the actual meat of the review, the concept of the game and the driving point of Orwell.

[h1] THE CHOICE IS YOURS[/h1]

The focus of what the developers are getting at is the whole anti-surveillance vs. freedom. The story hints you that the Nation (that is the country of this game) is trying to add more cameras after the safety bill was passed and some foreign problem that led to mass immigration, based on what the articles within the game said. The game even tried to give you signs that you are “supposedly” working for the bad guy and that the group that you were assigned to follow name [i]Thought[/i] is the good guys because they believe in Freedom of Speech and you are trying to incriminate them. How exactly you are incriminating them is because of how Orwell is set up to be. Orwell is a super-computer that analyze information and even interpret the information for you to post it. Unfortunately, because of how Orwell acts according to its programming it will translate the language the program will find it logical. Which leads to falsify the context that was given if you don’t read their messages clearly because remember, only you know the truth and Symes is only there as your advisor so he won’t know the full context of your side of the truth, only Orwell.  That is why it can be easy for people to get arrested just because Symes read what you send base on Orwell translated. Is this good?

 Well at first I almost had a problem with It because why the developers put it that way, but later as I finished the game I realized this was purposefully done this way and it was the right call. The purpose of their message is that people have way too much confidence of a machine to do their jobs for you they forgot how machines can be the dumbest tools for interpreting human language which they probably will never understand unless you are human. This is why in real life there are moderators to keep track of reports of people saying certain stuff. Bots can detect it but when humans actually read the context of their side of the story the problem is fix. The game did a great job of showing how humans rely on Orwell too much, but what I’m most impress is why they design the game to make it only you see the whole truth. 

In my playthrough I played the game like it was real life, I pretend I actually worked for the government and I role-play as an investigator, although sometimes I break my role to send certain data chunks that have nothing to do with the case but to pull Symes hair on certain funny comments. Anyway, when you sit down and do your “job” to be the eye on everyone’s business, not to joke around I felt pressure on taking the responsibility on sending people’s privacy, even if it means breaking some moral codes for the good of saving lives. I somehow felt like a god knowing people’s secrets and manipulate their lives on sending whatever data it comes and I send that data to Symes so that he take action to do something of this person. I can see why having this kind of power is utter madness to have, but at the same time is it really crazy to have this power?

 The game gives you a clear sense of black and white of giving you choices to follow, either be pro-government by pleasing them everything you send or follow your own thoughts of which is good and bad. Certainly, nobody here is good at least for the group [i]Thought[/i], I wish Symes would talk more of his stance of the government trying to make people safe like he would talk about how certain parts of giving up freedom for security is good even if they don’t understand. This would create an even more dilemma which the game has but certain parts fail which leads to my last discussion. 

How it handles the 1984 concepts. I felt they only scratch the surface of what it truly means for giving up your freedom. [i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens?

 Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation?  These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought.  

In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

The art style is another unique aspect of the game of how it shows a polygonal art style look. Most of the faces are fine though some were not as quite good in certain looks like some faces of the characters you profile are a bit strange with their beady eyes or mouth. The music is quite good giving you a sense of futuristic vibe to it while also gives you a dread feeling where certain events happen during your case. You even have one shot whatever you send data chunks to Symes and you can’t go back to it even exit the game won’t do. Whatever you send to Symes will affect the characters that you are working on the case. Which now I will talk about the actual meat of the review, the concept of the game and the driving point of Orwell. [h1] THE CHOICE IS YOURS[/h1] The focus of what the developers are getting at is the whole anti-surveillance vs. freedom. The story hints you that the Nation (that is the country of this game) is trying to add more cameras after the safety bill was passed and some foreign problem that led to mass immigration, based on what the articles within the game said. The game even tried to give you signs that you are “supposedly” working for the bad guy and that the group that you were assigned to follow name [i]Thought[/i] is the good guys because they believe in Freedom of Speech and you are trying to incriminate them. Unfortunately, because of how Orwell acts according to its programming it will translate the language the program will find it logical. Which leads to falsify the context that was given if you don’t read their messages clearly because remember, only you know the truth and Symes is only there as your advisor so he won’t know the full context of your side of the truth, only Orwell. That is why it can be easy for people to get arrested just because Symes read what you send base on Orwell translated. Is this good? The purpose of their message is that people have way too much confidence of a machine to do their jobs for you they forgot how machines can be the dumbest tools for interpreting human language which they probably will never understand unless you are human. This is why in real life there are moderators to keep track of reports of people saying certain stuff. Bots can detect it but when humans actually read the context of their side of the story the problem is fix. I can see why having this kind of power is utter madness to have, but at the same time is it really crazy to have this power? The game gives you a clear sense of black and white of giving you choices to follow, either be pro-government by pleasing them everything you send or follow your own thoughts of which is good and bad. Certainly, nobody here is good at least for the group [i]Thought[/i], I wish Symes would talk more of his stance of the government trying to make people safe like he would talk about how certain parts of giving up freedom for security is good even if they don’t understand. This would create an even more dilemma which the game has but certain parts fail which leads to my last discussion. How it handles the 1984 concepts. I felt they only scratch the surface of what it truly means for giving up your freedom. [i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens? Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation? These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought. In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Fantastic game, I can't praise it enough. Solid story, solid characters and character progression, appealing art style, and perfect general pacing. The soundtrack, works perfectly for it- being that it's essentially a solid, subtle repeat throughout the entire game really makes those times where it picks up stand out and feel that much more important.  I really, really hope to see more from this company. And, admittedly, would love it if this premise is revisited in some way. This is the best game I've played in a long, long time. Exactly what I've been looking for. I just couldn't stop playing. I'm kind of sad that I've completely finished it. 

Issues; 
Some of the dialogue becomes a bit broken depending on your choices. Oftentimes Symes and Delacroix mentioned information that I'd intentionally not given them, later on in the story. This only really becomes noticeable on replay-but it could be worked on. Nothing like this will ever be perfect--I'm never going to seriously complain about a choice game having little issues like this. There's just too much that would have to go into a game with so many variants it to make it possible. 
There were a few lingering spelling/grammatical errors, which, given the nature of the game (Internet, instant messaging/texting), didn't really bother me all that much. (Such as Harrison tried to "fell" instead of flee.) I see these things on real articles, it's no different.
There are some bugs present, but, they're clearly being revised and, honestly, aren't game-breaking at this point.

My personal ideas; I believe there could be a little work done on the pacing of the listener- real-time DOES make it all that much more immersive, but, when it comes to replayabilty, and just the general idea of it most likely having an adult player-base, who may only have an hour or so to play before going back to their day-to-day, I feel like there should be...maybe an additional option in the settings to modify speed or..something? It's easier, and more fulfilling to put a game down for a session if you feel you were able to hit a certain level of 'achievement.' You know, the pleasure centers of the brain and all. Maybe if it were simply a more fluid letter-by-letter or syllabalic instead of by completion of a word? I don't know. 
The only other thing I could possibly suggest, would be for, if ever this title is revisited or turned into a 'series' of sorts, that it be a little more flexible? The ability to freely investigate more than is necessary--even additional people. Perhaps just in a casual sense aside from the story, since there is a necessary feeling of a 'time pinch' in the game itself. I think a lot of the audience are people like me who just like to dig, so the chance to just..index on a larger scale would be quite entertaining. 
And, lastly, the ability to generate more datachunks? This could be messy territory, though. I think this would fall into the 'would require too much forethought to ever be possible' category, but it's an idea nontheless. The system is automated, clearly, but, the evaluator should have an option to deem other things appropriate for investigation. I know there were a few things that I would have loved to have flagged that just weren't an option.

My apologies, I'm just VERY excited and passionate about this title. Guys, play it!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is interesting, the UI is fantastic, but...

The writing doesn't work. Not to me, at least.

So the idea is, you're an anonymous member of the public working with a new program that's half google, half snooping software. You're assigned a case - the first one is about a bomb placed in a plaza, and thanks to surveillance cameras you're assigned to look up everything about a suspect. So far so good, right? There's the relevant question of whether it's right to spy on someone in the name of public safety, there's a mystery to solve...

But it falls apart. Your supervisor is all "she has a police record, let's snoop on her" and okay, good enough reason to investigate...her faux-facebook page, her faux-portfolio, news websites, etcetera. Except that none of these websites feel like they were ever used by real people, her facebook timeline feels bizarre, like she's a fascimile of a human being, and when you get to eavesdrop on her text messages with her boyfriend, again it feels false?

Everything is off, and not in a good way. And your supervisor is so ready to pin the entire case on her because she's joined an activist group that organizes protests against the surveillance state.

It's too on the nose, with writing that doesn't sell to me that I'm snooping on real people, with a wonky "this is taking place in real time" - but it's not, really, you only get to eavesdrop on people's text conversations when you unlock them, not when they happen - and it all just feels clumsy.

In a game that's only got its writing going for it, having a fantastically slick UI isn't going to keep me playing it. Which is a bummer! The questions this game is asking are relevant, and it's so slick and pretty to look at I want to dig into it! ... But sadly it's just not compelling.

Bummer.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If there were a "maybe" option for recommending this game I would have given it that, but with only a "yes" or "no" choice unfortunately I have to just come down on the side of the latter.

This game is essentially a "choose your own adventure" detective novel wherein your decisions are all made by choosing which information to share with - or conceal from - the authorities. The concept is an interesting one and the game does throw up some nice surprises in both the gameplay and the plot, and there are occasional moments of humour.

However, the limitations in using conflicting information are rather annoying. For example sometimes the game will let you choose only one of two (or more) different pieces of information even when both are true and could be vital to successfully completing your objectives. (I get that this is a key game mechanic, but I think it could be explained or handled better to make the game feel less forced.) In particular there is one key decision which just comes down to a 50/50 guess with no supporting information to help the player make the correct choice. (I am talking about the part where the player must determine the third location - If I missed any clues as to which is the correct answer, somebody please tell me!)

Another major concern is the quality of the writing; whilst for the most part the writing is capable and there are some memorable moments, the writing is never compelling - I gave up reading about halfway through my first playthrough, instead just scanning text for the (conveniently highlighted) choices. Whilst I can forgive bad writing in some games, for a game that is all about the writing the standard really needs to be higher. Some of the text simply drags on too long, especially any form of dialogue (phone calls, chat text, etc.) - this is doubly annoying for dialogue as there is no way to skip it. (Usually you can just let it run in the background whilst you read other in-game documents, but be careful with this as some actions are time-critical.)

Replay value may depend how willing you are to work through the text again. Whilst it is nice to see the different outcomes your actions can have, it feels like 90% or more of the game remains identical so it becomes a slog to see the few changes or pick up achievements. Some of the achievements are so ambiguously described that the only way to complete them seems to be relying on lots of replays and blind luck, or of course walkthroughs.

It is a shame to see such a nice idea and plot wasted without sufficient polish, but if the devs learn from this I do look forward to seeing what else they can produce.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Don't mind my playtime, I've played and finished this game on another platform so it's not counted here.
I can absolutely say that this game is very brilliant. From the UI design which makes you feel like you're really working from home on your own computer, to the story, which is very well written and developed.

The more you go on with the story, if you really pay attention to the details, the more the plot twist becames obvious, but it's certainly nothing you might expect from the beginning.

It's kinda short, and if you're not a fan of the genre it might be a little boring, since the things you do, except for those you can decide on, are actually driven and highlited by the game itself, so the interaction is almost limited to what the game wants you to do, but again, if you like the genre, the main feature of this game is actually the story, and the fact that you can discover it only bit by bit, by reading all the information given.

Currently this game is on sale, together with the second one in a bundle, and for less more than 4€ is totally a must-buy.

Small digression on the translation: I played the game with the Italian translation because that's my main language, the game started automatically in that language and it seemed ok in the beginning.
Sadly, the more it goes on, the more it gets worse. Some translated sentences are even totally senseless and sometimes it gets a little frustrating to read, since the game is based on reading info.
I understand that even if it's very bad it might be useful for people who can't read English, but I only wish I had a way to switch to English language in-game, so that I could have changed language while playing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Remember Spycraft: The Great Game? It was this weird mostly live-action-video adventure game that came on 4 cds back in the 90s, and tasked you to roll up an international conspiracy using your wits and a bunch of cool digital tools.

It played off "real" intelligence work, sifting through documents, collecting tidbits of data.

Orwell is a lot like that, but with just the digital shenanigans, played out in an age when the NSA sees you naked and knows who you're gossipping about.

I like it a lot, although it also kinda makes me miss the bits of Spycraft that felt realistic. Like sifting through a document in search of a password or a connection, having to really notice and remember details, and then piecing it all together yourself. 

It worked your brain and engaged you in a way that Orwell doesn't, but Orwell is so well put together that it makes up the difference. It keeps you hooked on the story and the taboo of looking through these peoples lives, sort of tapping into the "Facebook stalker" experience, thinking "God, what a loser" while you're tracing some two-bit musicians path into terrorism.

There are a couple of minor shortcomings though. There's no voice acting on phonecalls, sometimes you find relevant datapoints and you can't use them simply because they don't have "The Outline", and the conflict system can be a bit obtuse, not unlike the Lie/Doubt thing in LA Noire, which is frustrating, but never enough to bring the game down.

So if you want that experience of losing your soul in the service of a faceless controller-state that gives absolutely no fucks about you, then Orwell is about as good as it gets. Happy hunting, you mindless serfs!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them. • I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted. It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook. It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity. • The music acts as ambient background. It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy. This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge. [h1] Cons: [/h1] • Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings. It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game. If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads. If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through. What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat. • *Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent. They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention. If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact. Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified. You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent. • Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload. I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for. The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together. • Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently. Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait. The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before. • Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later. I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile. • It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away. For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information. • Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them. The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with. [h1] Conclusion: [/h1] Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely. Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us. Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force. This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power. A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice. An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction. True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries? We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted. These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion. If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer. Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review. You don't know who could be reading it. It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that. We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right? Oh crap, I hear them at my door. They're on to me! Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-! *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Wow I am more than impressed with this game. I am a big fan of the game genre of "Papers, Please", "This is the police" and similar games. I think when games explore your morals and hits you right in your cognitive dissonance. This game does this incredibly well. Surveilence is a difficult subject. There are pros and cons that vary between people.

This game sets your objective as having you aid in finding the suspect for a terrorist attack. This is of course a justifiable action and is in good favor for the public. You quickly start having conflicting thoughts about whether the people you're spying on and the information you gather is relevant at all. I am the type of person who is really interested in other people's affairs. This game absolutely worked wonders on this quirk of mine because I found it difficult to resist to look deeper in people's personal lives. I bet you will too constantly convince yourself that "this guy's past relationship drama might prove useful later".

The writing in this game is absolutely amazing in my honest opinion. This game felt real. The information layout, news articles, blogs, emails, texts, calls all felt real. The way you quickly progress from getting basic information on one person such as their name and occupation suddenly turns into having direct sneaky access to their desktop files, bank account activity and search history. You will find a lot of surprises in this game and lots of VERY difficult choices. There is a lot of conflicting ideas this game forces on you. For example you are presented with 2 or 3 very contradicting pieces of information. Sometimes it is easy to choose based on the source of where this info came from but when the consequences are severe, you are under pressure to make the right choice as there is no going back.

One downfall of this game is that there are some slight errors in the scripting that messes up the flow. For example there are certain bits which I suppose are meant to be discovered in a certain sequence but its possible to do it in the wrong sequence, resulting in dialogue that doesn't fit in. Alerting the higher ups of a threat after it already happened results in them thanking you for the useful information and that they will be prepared...even though this happened just recently and they were not prepared. The game also decides on itself which information is relevant or not and kind of makes you feel bad for collecting everything you might feel is necessary but thankfully you are not outright punished for it. Another big error I noticed was with relationships. I find out that a character has been married in the past and add it to the database but the database instead labels the character as currently married which is considered as wrong information until you find out more details later.

All in all these negatives do not affect the game much. This game is worth full price and I think is a must buy with a discount.

review_text_raw:
A lot of people are praising this game, but it's really simple. There are very few choices with usually obvious consiquences.

Most of the game feels like work. You click and drag the things that are highlighted and then the guy reveals more plot points and gives you more documents to read while you click and drag more stuff. It's made all the more painful by false "upload" times (really? Uploading text to the most complex security system ever takes 3+ seconds each time!? I understand people are interested in the story, or the greater point about surveillance, but as a game, this is just too simple. For a far better experience with a similar concept, I would highly suggest the ARG "This House Has People In It"

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The game advertises itself as a Big Brother simulator, but it doesn't [i]quite[/i] reach that level of depth and intrigue that kind of premise could reach.

However, I don't think Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You isn't a bad game at all. I think it's definitely a concept that is executed well. You play as an investigator who's collecting information on a variety of people through public channels, such as social media outlets, and private channels such as one's email. These pieces of information are used as evidence to solve the crime you're assigned to.

There is some decision-making in the game and it was interesting to see how the conversation changes between characters after performing certain actions. There are a couple of routes to take, but ultimately, the resolution is relatively the same. I don't mind this that much, and I honestly think true choice games are difficult to make, unless you have the resources as a studio.

However, the main element I found to be lacking was the story; it was rather light. There are a few tense moments in the story, but overall, it seemed like the writers decided on a safer route. I was expecting somewhat darker and more philosophical themes to be used in the game. They are touched upon lightly, but not expanded to play any significant role. Given the premise, there's a whole world of deep possibilities that could be played out, but the writing just scratches the surface of this. In the end, I found myself wanting a little more out of the game.

All in all, the game was less than satisfactory for me and I'd give it a neutral rating, if I could. If you're new to the whole 'mass surveillance' idea and want to see a taste of what a game could do with that idea, then sure, go play this. But if you want something deeper, this isn't quite it.

Side note: I also bought and played the DLC and it's just more of the same, in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
So Orwell nails the game as an interface in the same way the Hacker series does.

You're not a gamer sitting at your desk, your an employee doing your job.

Your job in this case is to sift through information - and decide what to pass on / or what not to pass on to your superiors who will act on it.

What you do or don't do can have drastic differences in outcomes - and while the game highlights data chunks for you - there is critical information found in other places the game does not highlight for you.

Timing is also important - you may early on get some interesting new data, but it might turn out later to be a red herring or even wrong - so a careful thought out approach to your investigation matters.

I've played through the first three episodes twice - with different 'role play' mentalities - and the differences can be huge.

It's a relatively short game, but well worth the price of entry and a fascinating look at privacy, security and rights in the digital age.

If you liked games like Hacker, Floor 13 (oldie but goodie), Papers Please - you'll find a lot to like here.

Some typos might throw you a bit - but they kind of ad to the experience.

Highly recommended, and an excellent price for a polished experience.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I believe Fellow Traveller Games is very interested in making people switch to Tails with giving away their published "Linux basics" game Hacknet for free (multiple times even!) first, and now give away this game too to fuel your paranoia and use some of that know-how to make you try and hide.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.
There is no way to change the font neither through options nor through config files, forum searches gave nothing in regards to that either, so be mindful of that.

Firstly this is a visual novel, so no super exciting and engaging gameplay is to be found, but honestly that may be for the better in these spying games.

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?
